title: 3 Simple Ways to Practice Classroom Management on Your Kids This Summer https://davestuartjr.com/3-simple-ways-to-practice-classroom-management-on-your-kids-this-summer
author: Mills Fabio, Lynsay
summary: Guest writer Lynsay Mills Fabio, a former ten-year classroom teacher and current parent, argues that summer break is a low-stakes training ground for the same classroom-management skills teachers need in the fall. She walks through three specific skills using parenting examples: giving clear directions using the SCOSM framework (Specific, Concrete, Observable, Sequential, with an optional Magic word), maintaining emotional constancy under provocation, and delivering consistent, pre-communicated consequences. Each section pairs a home example (bedtime routines with her son James) with the equivalent classroom application, explicitly tying the piece back to the Classroom Management Course she co-teaches with Dave Stuart Jr. The piece frames parenting mistakes and successes as direct practice reps for the classroom skills that matter most in the opening weeks of school.
points: SCOSM (Specific, Concrete, Observable, Sequential, optional Magic word) is presented as the core framework for giving directions that actually get followed, in both home and classroom settings.

Emotional Constancy -- staying pleasant and calm regardless of what a student (or child) brings through the door -- is framed as a trainable muscle, not a fixed trait, and visible annoyance is named as something that 'almost always makes things worse.'

Consistent, pre-communicated consequences (rule stated in advance, warning, then a concrete consequence) are presented as protecting 'everyone's right to learn and enjoy school' rather than as punitive.
The author's central argument is that the summer, with its lower stakes, is deliberate practice time for the exact classroom-management reps teachers will need in the fall.
quotes: I was a teacher for ten years. I’ve been a parent for four. When I make mistakes in parenting and wind up with a Whopper Freak Out, it’s almost always because I’m neglecting a basic tenet of good classroom management.

It’s the difference between “Go brush your teeth,” and “When I say ‘Go,' walk to the bathroom, pick up your blue toothbrush, take out the toothpaste, unscrew the cap, squeeze a tiny bit on the bristles, and brush back and forth. Ready? Go!
In our classrooms, we make the weather. We have to maintain a demeanor that is pleasant and likable no matter what baggage students bring through our doors or what emotions they let loose.
But the visible annoyance NEVER makes things better and almost always makes things worse. So we must practice a different response.
First, I make a clear rule: Stay in your own bed. If he breaks this rule and gets out of bed once, he gets a warning.
So this summer, practice giving a small consequence consistently. Pick an area of your day in which your kids are breaking a rule and driving you crazy. Name the clear rule and the consequence.
And you will, because you practiced on your own kids — or on nieces, nephews, and neighbors — all summer long.
